newsitem.title: USA: MORE BENIGN INFLATION EXPECTED IN JULY U.S. CPI.
newsitem.headline: MORE BENIGN INFLATION EXPECTED IN JULY U.S. CPI.

text.p: Predictions of low inflation have gone beyond the point of sounding like a broken record. Yet, Thursday's Consumer Price Index (CPI) report was again expected to show no visible signs of inflationary pressures.
"There is still lack of willingness of companies to push prices up," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities.
After rising 0.1 percent in June, the CPI was expected to rise 0.2 percent in July, with the core excluding food and energy also up 0.2 percent after a 0.1 percent gain in June.
"The economy is still very competitive. There is no evidence that wage costs are growing and nothing to suggest this environment is going to change," Iggo observed.

Except for a projected 0.6 percent rise in energy prices due to a rise in oil and gasoline prices, economists said most other prices look benign. Helping to contain prices, some noted, were widespread incentives at automobile dealerships.
"There are no pipeline pressures to make me think we will get bad news on inflation anytime soon," said Chris Probyn, economist at UBS Securities LLC.

The producer price index released on Tuesday showed wholesale prices at the finished goods level down for the seventh straight month, falling 0.1 percent in July. Both intermediate and crude goods also fell.
Similarly, consumer goods prices were benign, up 1.0 percent year-over-year fro, a 2.7 percent rise seen in January.
Services, though, have moved little, currently running at a 3.0 percent year-over-year rate from 3.3 percent at the beginning of the year.

One area that has piqued economists interests is medical benefit costs, which have steadily risen in recent months. Medical costs are now at an annualized 3.4 percent rate in 1997, up from 2.6 percent just a few months ago.
In June, medical costs were up 0.2 percent, preceeded by 0.3 percent, 0.3 percent and 0.4 percent, respecively, in May, April and March.
Before that, they were generally 0.2 percent or below.

"If sustained, it could continue to put modest pressure on core CPI but will also have an effect on the ECI (employment cost index)," said Ian Shepherdson, chief economist at HSBC Markets Inc. "It's nothing to get alarmed about no, but it is potentially interesting."
